# Miqsat Ma'ase Ha-Torah (4QMMT) — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Manuscripts** | 4Q394–4Q399, Cave 4, Qumran (six overlapping copies) |
| **Language** | Hebrew (Mishnaic-style) |
| **Date of Composition** | c. 150–125 BCE — possibly the earliest sectarian DSS text |
| **Genre** | Halakhic letter — a legal epistle from the Qumran leadership to the Jerusalem establishment |
| **Structure** | Three sections: A (calendar), B (legal rulings), C (closing appeal) |
| **Full Title** | *Miqsat Ma'ase Ha-Torah* — "Some Rulings Pertaining to the Torah" |
| **In One Sentence** | A formal letter from the Qumran community to the Jerusalem leadership — laying out approximately twenty specific points of legal disagreement, explaining why separation was necessary, and appealing for reconsideration — preserving, in passing, the very phrase Paul argues against in Galatians and Romans. |

---

## Sections Overview

MMT is reconstructed from six overlapping manuscripts (4Q394–399), none of which is complete. The composite text is divided by scholars into three sections:

- **Section A (the Calendar)**: Approximately nine columns presenting the 364-day solar calendar that the Qumran community followed. This section survives only partially and is the most reconstructed. The calendar was not merely a practical matter; following the wrong calendar meant observing holy days on the wrong days, which for this community constituted a form of fundamental religious error.

- **Section B (the Legal Rulings — Halakhot)**: The heart of the document. Approximately twenty specific legal rulings on which the community disagrees with the Jerusalem establishment. Topics include: purity of liquids flowing between vessels (the "pouring streams" controversy), the red heifer ceremony, the fitness of the blind and deaf to participate in the holy congregation, marriage among priests, bringing Gentile offerings to the temple, and others. Each ruling is stated with the formula "we hold that..." or "we think concerning..." — the plural first person throughout.

- **Section C (the Closing Appeal)**: A rhetorical climax addressed in the second person singular to a specific leader — likely the High Priest or a king. The appeal cites biblical examples of blessing and curse (Deuteronomy), calls for the recipient to study what has been written, and closes with one of the most theologically loaded sentences in the entire Scrolls corpus: "...and it will be reckoned to you as righteousness, when you do what is upright and good before him" (cf. Genesis 15:6).

---

## The World Behind the Text

To understand MMT, you must understand what the Qumran community was separating from — and why.

The Second Temple period (c. 516 BCE–70 CE) was not religiously unified. The dominant institutions — the Temple, its priesthood, the sacrificial system — were contested at every level. By the 2nd century BCE, at least three identifiable groups had formed distinct halakhic (legal) positions: the **Sadducees**, who held an aristocratic, conservative interpretation of the written Torah and denied oral tradition; the **Pharisees**, who developed an "oral Torah" of interpretation and were more popular with the common people; and the community at Qumran (often associated with the **Essenes**), who regarded both groups as corrupt and who maintained a strict, priest-centered interpretation of the law. There were also the **Hellenizers** — Jews who had accommodated to Greek culture — and the general mass of the population who followed no particular school.

The legal disputes in MMT Section B correspond closely to disputes known from rabbinic literature to have been argued between the Sadducees and the Pharisees. This is significant: the Qumran community appears, on some questions, to side with Sadducean positions against the Pharisees. This complicates any simple identification of Qumran with the Essenes of ancient reports, and it suggests that the legal landscape of early Judaism was more complex than any two-party model allows.

MMT's opening formula — "these are some of our rulings concerning the Torah" (*miqsat ma'ase ha-Torah*) — is written in a formal epistolary style. The text is a letter, addressed to someone in authority in Jerusalem, written in the authoritative plural of the community's leadership. It presents itself not as a polemical tract but as a formal legal communication between parties who share a common commitment to Torah — but who disagree on its implementation. The tone, notably, is not contemptuous. It is urgent, concerned, appealing. "We have separated from the majority of the people" — yes; but we are writing to you, which means we believe you might still be persuadable.

The 364-day calendar (Section A) deserves special attention. The standard Jewish calendar is lunisolar (approximately 354 days, adjusted with leap months). The Qumran community followed a strictly solar 364-day calendar, also attested in Jubilees and the Astronomical Book of 1 Enoch. On this calendar, the major festivals always fall on the same day of the week — Passover always on a Wednesday, for instance. The community believed this calendar was the correct one commanded at creation, and that the Jerusalem temple was observing the wrong festival dates. This was not a minor procedural disagreement. For a community centered on the sanctity of the liturgical calendar, observing the wrong dates made the Jerusalem cult fundamentally invalid.

---

## Why This Text Was Written

MMT appears to be a founding document — or close to it. It may represent the moment of formal separation between the group that became the Qumran community and the Jerusalem establishment. The language "we have separated from the majority of the people" (Section C) is not a statement of accomplished fact looking back; it reads like a declaration that is being made in the act of writing.

The purpose is threefold:
1. **Legal** — to state the community's positions on specific halakhic disputes and demonstrate their scriptural basis.
2. **Rhetorical** — to persuade the addressee (and, implicitly, the community itself) that the separation is legitimate and necessary.
3. **Theological** — the closing appeal ties legal obedience to righteousness before God, invoking the covenantal logic of Deuteronomy (blessing and curse) and the Abrahamic promise of Genesis 15:6.

The text is also, in some sense, a record of grievances. Writing things down is a way of saying: these matters are serious enough to be preserved. The community expected its rulings to be vindicated eventually — at the eschatological judgment, when the truth would be revealed and the righteous community would be recognized.

---

## How to Read This Text

Read MMT in three movements.

**Section A (the Calendar)** is the most difficult because it is the most fragmentary and most technical. If you find it opaque, skim it and focus on the key fact: the community used a different calendar from Jerusalem, and this was a fundamental religious disagreement, not an administrative quirk.

**Section B (the Rulings)** is the most historically informative section. Each ruling is short — often a single paragraph — and follows a consistent logic: here is what the Torah says, here is how it should be applied, here is what Jerusalem is doing wrong. You do not need to be a specialist in ancient Jewish law to follow the general argument. What you are reading is a meticulous, serious legal community working through specific problems of purity and holiness with intense attention to the text of scripture. These are not people who dismissed the Torah; they believed they were following it more faithfully than anyone else.

**Section C (the Appeal)** is the most emotionally charged section and the one with the most direct connections to the New Testament. Read it slowly. The appeal to the addressee — you know the history, you know what happens when Israel obeys and when it disobeys, consider our rulings, act righteously — is a sophisticated piece of theological rhetoric. The closing sentence about being "reckoned as righteousness" is a deliberate echo of Genesis 15:6 (God reckoned Abraham's trust as righteousness), applying the Abrahamic model to legal obedience. Paul will engage exactly this territory in Galatians and Romans — but from the opposite direction.

---

## The Threads — How This Text Connects

**Galatians 2:16 / Romans 3:28 — "works of the law" (erga nomou / ma'ase ha-Torah)**. This is the most important connection in the Scrolls for Pauline scholarship, and it transformed the field. Before MMT was published (1984 preliminary; full edition 1994), scholars debated what Paul meant by "works of the law" — were they generic moral deeds? The whole Torah? Ritual observances? MMT shows that *ma'ase ha-Torah* was a real, technical, pre-Christian Jewish phrase referring specifically to **particular halakhic rulings** — the kind of specific legal positions detailed in Section B. When Paul says "a person is not justified by works of the law (erga nomou) but through faith in Jesus Christ," he is using vocabulary that his Jewish contemporaries would have recognized as referring to specific legal rulings governing temple purity, calendar observance, and communal separation. He is not arguing against "trying hard to be good." He is engaging a specific strand of Second Temple legal theology. MMT does not tell us what Paul means — Paul is making his own argument — but it shows us the linguistic world Paul inhabited.

**Genesis 15:6** — "And he believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." MMT Section C closes with a near-quotation of this verse. Paul quotes the same verse in Galatians 3:6 and Romans 4:3, and it is central to his entire argument about faith and righteousness. Both Paul and the MMT author are reading Genesis 15:6 as foundational for the question of how one stands rightly before God. They reach opposite conclusions — MMT applies the logic to legal compliance; Paul applies it to faith apart from legal compliance. But the exegetical starting point is the same verse. Reading MMT alongside Galatians and Romans turns a one-sided debate into a conversation.

**The 364-day calendar** in MMT connects to the **Book of Jubilees** and the **Astronomical Book of 1 Enoch** (1 Enoch 72–82), both of which argue for the solar calendar. The calendar dispute is not unique to Qumran; it was part of a broader priestly tradition that predates the community. The Qumran community's self-understanding as the correct observers of the festival calendar also informs how they read prophetic texts about the "appointed times" (*mo'adim*) of God.

**Sadducean halakhah**: Several of MMT's legal rulings in Section B correspond closely to positions attributed to the Sadducees in rabbinic literature (particularly in the Mishnah tractate Yadaim and in Tosefta sources). The "pouring streams" ruling (that liquid poured between vessels can transmit impurity) is one of the clearest examples. This connection has led some scholars to argue that MMT represents a Sadducean or proto-Sadducean legal tradition, or that the Qumran community's origins lie closer to priestly Sadducean circles than to the Essenes of Josephus's description.

**Deuteronomy 28–30 (blessing and curse)** provides the theological framework for Section C. The appeal to the addressee works entirely within the covenantal logic of Deuteronomy: obey and be blessed, disobey and be cursed; Israel's history of exile and restoration is evidence of this pattern; now is the time to obey and be restored. The use of Deuteronomy in MMT is sophisticated and presupposes an audience saturated in the biblical text.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

- **MMT is the only Qumran text written as a letter.** Every other major sectarian text is either a rule, a pesher, a hymn, a liturgy, or a legal code. MMT is an epistle — addressed to a specific person, making a specific argument, seeking a specific response. This is remarkable because it implies an original moment of appeal, a belief that dialogue was still possible. Whatever subsequent separation occurred, MMT represents a point at which the community believed the Jerusalem establishment could be persuaded. That belief apparently died with the text — no response survives, and the community did not return to Jerusalem.

- **The "works of the law" discovery was the most significant Pauline scholarship development of the 20th century.** This is not an exaggeration. E. P. Sanders's 1977 book *Paul and Palestinian Judaism* had already begun to challenge the Lutheran reading of Paul (in which "works of the law" = earning salvation by moral effort). When MMT was published and the technical phrase *ma'ase ha-Torah* became known, it corroborated a reading of Paul in which his arguments were engaged with specific halakhic debates rather than with generic legalism. James Dunn's "new perspective on Paul" and N. T. Wright's extensive treatments both take MMT as foundational evidence. Understanding this background does not resolve how to read Paul — the debates continue fiercely — but it changes the questions.

- **Six copies of MMT survived.** The Dead Sea Scrolls typically preserve one to a handful of copies of any given text. Six copies of MMT suggests this document was copied and studied extensively within the community. It was not an archival document; it was in active use. The community apparently regarded it as foundational — perhaps as the founding letter of the movement.

- **The "pouring streams" (torat ha-nisoq) controversy** in Section B is both arcane and revealing. The question is: if you pour liquid from a pure vessel into an impure vessel, does the impurity travel back up the stream into the pure vessel? The Pharisees said no; the MMT community said yes. This sounds like the most esoteric possible dispute, but it governed everyday behavior around food preparation and ritual washing. For a community centered on purity, getting this wrong meant everything in your kitchen could make you impure. The stakes were total — not because the community was obsessive, but because purity was how you maintained standing in the presence of the holy God.

- **The addressee is unnamed and debated.** Section C is addressed in the second person singular — "you" — to a single leader. Who is it? The most common answers are: the High Priest (possibly Jonathan or Simon Maccabaeus), or the Hasmonean ruler. The text never names him, which may mean the original recipients knew perfectly well who the letter was for, or it may mean the community kept the letter as a template for future appeals. Either way, the unnamed "you" is a historical person who received this letter — and who apparently did not respond as the community hoped.

- **"We have separated from the majority of the people"** (Section C) is the community's own description of itself. They chose separation; they did not experience it as exile alone. This phrase is crucial: it shows a community with agency, making a principled decision, not merely a group that was expelled. The decision to separate was theological, legal, and deliberate.

---

## Why This Text Isn't in Your Bible

MMT is a sectarian legal letter, not scripture. Like all the pesharim and community documents from Qumran, it was never a candidate for any biblical canon. It was written by a specific Jewish community in the 2nd century BCE, addressed to a specific audience, on specific legal questions — and then hidden in a cave when that community was destroyed in 68 CE.

Its significance for anyone who reads the New Testament is indirect but profound: it illuminates the vocabulary and the debates that Paul was engaging. MMT helps us read Galatians and Romans more accurately. But it is not itself scripture; it is evidence — some of the most important evidence we have — for the world in which the New Testament was written.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 175–163 BCE | Antiochus IV Epiphanes; Hellenistic crisis in Jerusalem |
| c. 152 BCE | Jonathan Maccabaeus assumes high priesthood — possible precipitating event for Qumran separation |
| c. 150–125 BCE | Probable composition of MMT; community separation from Jerusalem |
| c. 50–68 CE | Copying of the six surviving MMT manuscripts |
| c. 68 CE | Roman destruction of Qumran; manuscripts hidden in Cave 4 |
| 1947–1952 CE | Discovery of Cave 4; MMT fragments recovered |
| 1984 CE | Elisha Qimron and John Strugnell preliminary announcement; first publication of the phrase *ma'ase ha-Torah* |
| 1994 CE | Full critical edition published (DJD X, Qimron and Strugnell) |

---

*— HESED, Reader's Guide Division*
